content: 1. Women with prediabetes or diabetes should be carefully monitored when using oral contraceptives due to potential metabolic effects. 2. A small percentage of women may experience persistent hypertriglyceridemia while taking oral contraceptives. 3. Changes in serum triglycerides and lipoprotein levels have been reported in users of oral contraceptives, as previously discussed in warnings. 4. Clinical studies with MonoNessa® did not show any clinically significant changes in fasting blood glucose levels. 5. Over 24 cycles of use, no statistically significant changes in mean fasting blood glucose levels were observed. 6. Glucose tolerance tests revealed minimal and clinically insignificant changes from baseline to cycles 3, 12, and 24. 7. Women with significant hypertension should not initiate hormonal contraception. 8. 9. Data from the Royal College of General Practitioners and subsequent trials indicate that the incidence of hypertension increases with higher progestational activity. 10. Women with a history of hypertension, hypertension-related diseases, or renal disease should be encouraged to use alternative contraceptive methods. 11. 12. Women who develop hypertension during hormonal contraceptive therapy should generally switch to a non-hormonal contraceptive method. 13. If non-hormonal methods are unsuitable, hormonal contraceptive therapy may continue with concurrent antihypertensive treatment. 14. 15. 16. 17. The onset or worsening of migraines, or the development of recurrent, persistent, or severe headaches, requires discontinuation of oral contraceptives and evaluation of the underlying cause. 18. Breakthrough bleeding and spotting may occur in patients using oral contraceptives, especially during the first three months of use. 19. 20. If pathology is excluded, time or a change to another formulation may resolve the issue. 21. In cases of amenorrhea, pregnancy should be ruled out. 22. Some women may experience post-pill amenorrhea or oligomenorrhea, particularly if such conditions were preexisting. 23. Ectopic and intrauterine pregnancies may occur in cases of contraceptive failure. 24. Patients should be counseled that oral contraceptives do not protect against HIV infection (AIDS) or other sexually transmitted diseases. 25. Annual history and physical examinations are recommended for all women, including those using oral contraceptives. 26. Physical examinations may be deferred until after initiating oral contraceptives if deemed appropriate by the clinician and requested by the patient. 27. 28. 29. Women with a strong family history of breast cancer or breast nodules should be monitored with particular care. 30. Women being treated for hyperlipidemias should be closely monitored if they choose to use oral contraceptives. 31. Some progestogens may elevate LDL levels and make hyperlipidemia management more challenging. 32. If jaundice develops in a woman receiving oral contraceptives, the medication should be discontinued. 33. Steroid hormones may be poorly metabolized in patients with impaired liver function. 34. Oral contraceptives may cause fluid retention and should be prescribed cautiously in patients with conditions that could be aggravated by fluid retention. 35. Women with a history of depression should be carefully observed, and the medication should be discontinued if depression recurs to a serious degree. 36. Contact lens wearers who develop visual changes or changes in lens tolerance should be assessed by an ophthalmologist. 37. Oral contraceptives may affect certain endocrine and liver function tests, as well as blood components, including increased prothrombin and clotting factors (VII, VIII, IX, X), decreased antithrombin III, and increased norepinephrine-induced platelet aggregability. 38. Thyroid-binding globulin (TBG) levels may increase, leading to elevated circulating total thyroid hormone levels, though free T4 concentrations remain unchanged. 39. Other serum-binding proteins may also be elevated. 40. Sex hormone-binding globulins may increase, resulting in elevated total circulating sex steroids, though free or biologically active levels may decrease or remain unchanged. 41. Triglyceride levels may increase, and other lipid and lipoprotein levels may be affected. 42. Glucose tolerance may decrease. 43. Serum folate levels may be depressed by oral contraceptive therapy, which could be clinically significant if a woman becomes pregnant shortly after discontinuing oral contraceptives. 44. Serious adverse reactions associated with oral contraceptive use include thrombophlebitis, venous thrombosis with or without embolism, arterial thromboembolism, pulmonary embolism, myocardial infarction, cerebral hemorrhage, cerebral thrombosis, hypertension, gallbladder disease, hepatic adenomas, and benign liver tumors. 45. There is evidence of an association between oral contraceptive use and mesenteric thrombosis and retinal thrombosis. 46. Adverse reactions believed to be drug-related include nausea, vomiting, gastrointestinal symptoms (e.g., abdominal cramps, bloating), breakthrough bleeding, spotting, changes in menstrual flow, amenorrhea, temporary infertility after discontinuation, edema, melasma (which may persist), breast changes (tenderness, enlargement, secretion), weight changes (increase or decrease), changes in cervical erosion and secretion, diminished lactation when given immediately postpartum, cholestatic jaundice, migraine, and allergic reactions (e.g., rash, urticaria, angioedema).
